summary: Provides guidance on how the ITU-T and the Internet Society and IETF collaborate on standards development. It reflects changes in both organizations since RFC 2436, which it replaces, and much of its text is shared with the ITU-T. It was later replaced by RFC 6756.

plainLanguage.summary: Two big groups that write technical rules sometimes work on the same subjects. This document explains how they should cooperate so they do not step on each other.

questions: how do the ietf and itu-t collaborate
what are the ietf itu-t collaboration guidelines
subtitle: How two major standards organizations coordinate their work on overlapping topics.

tldr.problem: Both the IETF and the ITU-T set standards for Internet and telecommunications. They sometimes work on the same topics, and need a way to coordinate to avoid conflicts and duplication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC establishes formal processes for the organizations to share information about their work, communicate through designated contact points, exchange draft documents, and reference each other's specifications appropriately.
tldr.outcome: Clear procedures help the organizations collaborate effectively while maintaining their independence. The document was replaced by RFC 6756 with updated guidance.

today: RFC 3356 is an Informational RFC from August 2002 that was obsoleted by RFC 6756 in January 2013. It provided guidance on collaboration between the IETF and the ITU-T; RFC 6756 provides updated guidance reflecting changes in both organizations since this RFC was written.

sections.title: Why IETF and ITU-T Need to Collaborate
sections.content:
The Internet and telecommunications worlds have converged. Both the Internet Society's Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) and the International Telecommunication Union's Telecommunications Standardization Sector (ITU-T) now write standards for technologies that overlap, such as signaling, routing, security, and IP-based networks. Rather than working in isolation, the two organizations formally agreed to coordinate their efforts so they can bring their separate expertise to bear effectively.

This RFC provides guidance on how the two organizations should interact. It updates an earlier version (RFC 2436) to reflect changes in both organizations' procedures and structure since 1998.
sections.plainLanguage: Both groups set rules for how computers talk. They decided to tell each other what they are working on so the same rules do not get written twice in different ways.

sections.title: How the Organizations Track Each Other's Work
sections.content:
Each organization maintains lists of its current work. The IETF publishes draft charters for new working groups to a mailing list called IETF NewWork. The ITU-T subscribes to this list so its Study Groups can watch for topics of mutual interest. When the ITU-T begins new work, it sends updates to the same mailing list so the IETF can identify overlaps.

When a potential collaboration area is identified, representatives from the two organizations make contact through designated leaders: IETF Area Directors correspond with ITU-T Study Group Chairmen, and IETF Working Group Chairs correspond with ITU-T Rapporteurs. This ensures that coordination happens at the appropriate level of authority.
sections.plainLanguage: Each group posts a list of what they are working on. If they see something interesting, they send a message to the other group's leaders.

sections.title: Representation and Formal Communication
sections.content:
The IETF and ITU-T recognize each other's delegates. The Internet Society is a Sector Member of the ITU-T, so IETF representatives can attend ITU-T meetings as ISOC delegates. ITU-T Study Group Chairmen can authorize members to attend IETF meetings as official ITU-T delegates speaking on behalf of their groups.

Formal communication between the organizations must be explicitly approved and properly routed. Messages from the ITU-T to the IETF are addressed to working group chairs and area directors with a copy to statements@ietf.org, where they are recorded on a liaison statements web page. This prevents miscommunication and ensures decisions are properly documented.
sections.plainLanguage: Members can go to the other group's meetings as official guests. If one group wants to send a message to the other, it goes through the leaders and gets written down.

sections.title: Sharing and Cross-Referencing Documents
sections.content:
The two organizations can share working drafts. An IETF working group can submit Internet Drafts to the ITU-T as contributions from ISOC, but only after the working group agrees it is worthwhile and the appropriate Area Directors approve. Similarly, the ITU-T can submit draft Recommendations to the IETF as Internet Drafts, and this is often done simultaneously by both organizations on topics of mutual interest.

The organizations use each other's documents as references rather than creating joint documents. ITU-T Recommendations can reference IETF RFCs, and RFCs can reference ITU-T Recommendations. This allows each organization to maintain its own approval and revision procedures while still benefiting from the other's work.
sections.plainLanguage: They can share their work-in-progress documents with each other. They can also mention each other's finished documents in their own, like footnotes in a book.

sections.title: Current Status
sections.content: RFC 3356 is an Informational document that was published in August 2002 and obsoletes RFC 2436. It was itself obsoleted and replaced by RFC 6756 with updated guidance. The procedures it describes have been the foundation for practical collaboration between the two organizations on IP-based technologies and remain relevant to their ongoing coordination.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is informational (not a technical standard) and is now historical. A newer version with updated rules is RFC 6756.
